column7: I can help promote IEEE RAS through social media content, technical reels, interactive workshops, coding challenges, and student engagement activities. I also believe fun technical events and beginner-friendly sessions can attract more students to the community.

I believe the best way to grow a technical community is to make it approachable, engaging, and genuinely exciting rather than limiting it to only formal workshops or competitions. One unconventional way I would help promote IEEE RAS is by creating a “build culture” instead of just an “event culture.” Many students hesitate to join technical communities because they think they need advanced skills beforehand. I would focus on creating beginner-friendly mini-project spaces where people can casually experiment, fail, learn, and collaborate without feeling intimidated.
Another idea would be to organize short interactive sessions around practical engineering concepts rather than only theoretical talks. For example, sessions involving hardware teardown analysis, robotics demonstrations, Linux customization workshops, automation setups, AI applications, or “how things actually work” discussions could attract students who are curious but unsure where to start. These kinds of sessions make technology feel more accessible and exciting.
I also think social media promotion can be made more creative. Instead of only posting announcements, IEEE RAS could share project showcases, member spotlights, behind-the-scenes development processes, technical myths, quick engineering facts, or progress logs from ongoing projects. This makes the community feel active and relatable rather than just event-focused.
Another unconventional approach would be collaborative cross-domain projects involving robotics, AI, software, embedded systems, and sustainability-oriented ideas. Since many students have interests beyond traditional robotics, combining domains can bring in a wider audience and create more innovation within the community.
Finally, I believe consistency matters more than occasional large events. A community grows strongest when members feel involved regularly, whether through discussions, collaborative learning spaces, project circles, or informal technical interactions.

To build and promote the IEEE RAS community in MUJ in unconventional and engaging ways, I believe the focus should be on making robotics and automation more interactive, relatable, and accessible to students from all backgrounds, not just those with prior technical experience.

One innovative approach could be organizing “Tech-in-Real-Life” campaigns where the community demonstrates how robotics and automation are already influencing daily life, such as AI assistants, smart devices, autonomous systems, and healthcare technologies. Instead of limiting activities to traditional workshops, we can create short live demonstrations in common campus areas to attract curiosity and encourage students to participate.

Another unconventional idea would be hosting “Build Nights” or “Midnight Innovation Sessions,” where students collaborate casually on mini projects, brainstorming sessions, or robotics challenges in a relaxed environment. These events would create a strong sense of community and encourage students to interact beyond formal academic settings. Peer learning can often be more effective and motivating than conventional classroom learning.

Social media can also be used creatively by producing short-form content, behind-the-scenes project videos, student success stories, technical memes, quizzes, and interactive reels related to robotics and automation. Instead of only posting announcements, the goal would be to make the IEEE RAS page entertaining, informative, and highly engaging for students.

Collaborating with non-technical clubs could also significantly expand outreach. For example, combining robotics with gaming, design, entrepreneurship, or sustainability can help students from different interests connect with the community. Organizing robotics-based treasure hunts, automation-themed competitions, or campus-wide tech challenges can make participation exciting and memorable.

Additionally, mentorship circles where seniors guide beginners in small groups could help students feel more comfortable entering the technical domain. Many students hesitate because they think robotics is too advanced, so building a welcoming and beginner-friendly culture is essential.

Overall, I believe the best way to grow the IEEE RAS community is by making it inclusive, creative, interactive, and student-driven. When people enjoy being part of a community and feel that they are learning in a fun and supportive environment, growth and engagement naturally follow.
